meta.title: CipherMesh — end-to-end encrypted terminal chat
meta.description: A terminal chat where encryption is the product. The relay only ever sees ciphertext: it cannot read, alter or fake anything. Free and open source.

hero.title: The server can't read a single word.
hero.lead: CipherMesh is a chat that lives in your terminal. Messages are encrypted on your machine and decrypted on your friend's. The relay in between only forwards sealed envelopes — it has no way to open them.
hero.relayNote: Same message, both sides. The envelope is padded to a fixed size, so its length says nothing about what is inside — and it is not signed with a name, so the relay cannot tell who sent it.

transcript.text: the key never leaves this machine
so the relay only ever moves noise?

proof.title: Not a prototype
proof.lead: Every line below is checkable in the repository.

values.commands: {commands} in the client, {p2p} of them offline too
values.license: MIT — fork it, run it, read it

replay.title: A whole session, start to wiped
replay.lead: Everything else on this page describes CipherMesh. This is it running: connect to the hub, prove who is on the other end, say something, then wipe the disk. It is a recording rather than a video — every line is text the client actually prints, replayed in the browser.

verbatim.name: The strings are the client's
verbatim.body: Every system, info and error line here is copied out of the client's source rather than written for the page. If one of them changes in a future release, this goes stale in a way somebody will notice.

derived.name: The key art is computed
derived.body: The randomart block is not a screenshot. The browser runs the same drunken-bishop walk the terminal runs, over the same demo key, so the picture cannot drift away from the algorithm it is showing.

nothing.name: A few kilobytes of text
nothing.body: A video would not follow the theme, would blur on a phone and would go stale silently. Text stays sharp at any size, costs almost nothing to load, and a screen reader can read the whole session.

features.title: What you get
features.lead: Every one of these is in the client today — not a roadmap.

pq.name: Hybrid post-quantum
pq.body: X25519 plus ML-KEM-768, mixed into the ratchet root. Traffic recorded today stays unreadable to a future quantum computer, and security never drops below the classical construction.

pfs.name: Perfect forward secrecy
pfs.body: A Double Ratchet gives every single message its own key. Compromising a device today does not open yesterday's conversations.

sealed.name: Sealed sender
sealed.body: The relay does not even learn who sent a message. Add fixed-bucket padding and optional cover traffic and it cannot tell chatting from idle.

rooms.name: Private rooms
rooms.body: Password-protected rooms where the password never leaves your machine. The server stores only a verifier, in memory, and the room dies with its last member.

buffers.name: Multi-room buffers
buffers.body: Be in several rooms at once and switch with Alt+1..9. Which room a message belongs to travels inside the encrypted payload — the relay never learns it.

p2p.name: Serverless P2P
p2p.body: Drop the relay entirely: peers find each other over mDNS on the local network, with nearly the same command set.

security.title: What the operator can and cannot do
security.lead: This is worth being blunt about, because it is the whole point of the design.

cannot.hand: Hand over content that does not exist in readable form

security.footnote: Rooms exist only while someone is inside them. When the last person leaves, the room and everything said in it are gone — there is nothing to hand over later.

start.title: Running in under a minute
start.lead: No account, no signup, nothing to install permanently.

run.name: Run it
run.body: Node 20 or newer is all you need.

connect.name: Point it at a relay
connect.body: Type ciphermesh.de at the server prompt to use the public hub, or run your own with npx ciphermesh server.

talk.name: Agree on a room
talk.body: Both of you type the same room name and you are talking. Add a password to make it private.

start.demoAlt: The CipherMesh client running in a terminal: a room list, an encrypted conversation and the command bar.
start.selfhost: Prefer your own? The repository ships a Docker setup that gets a Let's Encrypt certificate automatically.

community.title: Now there is somewhere to meet
community.lead: For a long time, using CipherMesh meant already knowing someone who ran a relay. That changed: ciphermesh.de is a public hub anyone can connect to, free, and it is where the project's community happens.

presence.online: {range} people in the hub right now
presence.empty: Nobody in the hub right now — be the first

community.connectNote: That is the whole join flow. The hub is always on, so there is no need to coordinate who starts the server.

open.name: Rooms anyone can open
open.body: Pick a name, tell the people you want in it, start talking. No account, no invitation, no waiting list.

general.name: Everyone lands in general
general.body: The default room is where to go if you just want to see who else is around. Say hello — it is the closest thing the project has to a front door.

private.name: Private the moment you want it
private.body: Add a password and the room is yours. The password never reaches the server, only a verifier it cannot reverse.

ephemeral.name: Nothing outlives the conversation
ephemeral.body: A room exists while someone is inside it. When the last person leaves it is gone — no history, no archive, nothing anyone could hand over.

community.purposeBody: The hub is a meeting point: it exists so you can try CipherMesh and find other people using it without running a server first. It is not a general-purpose communications service — rooms are nobody's home, there are no accounts, and nothing is kept between sessions.
community.selfhostTitle: Need more? Then the relay should be yours
community.selfhostBody: A relay you host answers to you, depends on nobody else's uptime, and does not put your conversations through a machine a stranger administers. The repository ships the Docker setup ready to go. For anything that matters it is the better answer — and it is the one the software was built for.
community.note: Running the hub does not make its operator a reader. It is zero-knowledge like every other CipherMesh relay — the only difference is that this one is always on.

verify.title: Encryption is only half of it
verify.lead: Sealing a message protects it from the relay. It says nothing about who is holding the other key. CipherMesh makes that check something you can finish in about ten seconds.

match.title: The same code on both screens.
match.body: Neither side sent the code to the other — both derived it from the two public keys. They can only agree if those keys are the real ones, so there is no third key in the path. Confirm with /verify-confirm rita and the client remembers from then on.

differ.title: Different codes. Stop here.
differ.body: Each side is holding a key belonging to the machine in between, so each is hashing a different pair. Everything else looks normal — the chat works, the names are right — and this is the only thing that gives it away. Do not confirm, and reach the person another way.

check.note: Illustrative keys. The browser hashes with SHA-256 because it has no BLAKE2b; the client uses BLAKE2b-256. The construction is the client's: sort both public keys, hash them with a domain separator, read five bytes as thirteen digits grouped 4-4-5.

sas.name: Compare thirteen digits
sas.body: Both sides derive the same short code from the two public keys. Read it out on a call or hold up the QR the client prints. If the codes match, nobody is standing in the middle.

outofband.name: Never typed back
outofband.body: The code is only ever compared by humans, on a channel that is not this one. There is nothing to enter, so there is nothing for an attacker to replay.

tofu.name: The client remembers for you
tofu.body: A peer's key is pinned the first time you see it. If it ever changes, you are warned before you type the next message — not after.

verify.note: /fingerprint prints your own, /trustlist shows everyone you have confirmed. None of this is buried in a settings screen.

limits.title: What this does not protect
limits.lead: Encryption is a narrow promise, and a page that lists only strengths is asking you to trust a sales pitch. None of this is new — it is in SECURITY.md and in section 2 of the terms — but it belongs where people actually read.

address.name: Your network address
address.body: It has to route packets somewhere. Put Tor or a VPN in front if that matters to you, or run /p2p and take the relay out of the picture entirely.

identity.name: Your nickname and public key
identity.body: A room has to route to somebody. A nickname is not an authenticated identity, which is exactly why verification exists.

shape.name: When you talk, and roughly how much
shape.body: Content is sealed and padded into fixed buckets, but timing and bucket size still travel. Sealed sender hides who sent a message from an honest-but-curious relay; a hostile one can still tie a socket to a session.

endpoint.name: A device someone else is holding
endpoint.body: If somebody has your machine while it is unlocked, they have the plaintext. End-to-end means the ends, and your end is one of them.

exported.name: /export writes plaintext
exported.body: It is your data and the command is explicit, but the file it produces carries none of the protection the conversation had.

names.name: Names prove nothing
names.body: Anyone can call themselves anything. Trust attaches to keys, through pinning and SAS, and never to a nickname.

sent.name: Anything already delivered
sent.body: It wipes your disk, not theirs. A message the other side received sits on their machine and stays there.

copies.name: Copies you made yourself
copies.body: Exports, screenshots and pasted text are outside the client's reach the moment they exist.

memory.name: That you connected at all
memory.body: Operational logs record connections and room events — never content — and are deleted after at most seven days.

limits.close: If any of that is unacceptable for what you are doing, this is the wrong tool. Saying so here is better than you finding out after relying on it.

versus.title: Why not just use Signal?
versus.lead: Most people should use Signal. It is audited, it is maintained by people paid to maintain it, and it runs on the phone already in your pocket. This is not competing with that — it answers a different question.

items.phone: You want the thing your family will actually install and keep using.
items.audited: You want formally reviewed cryptography with a funded team behind it.
items.everyone: Handing over a phone number to register is not a problem for you.

items.lan: There is no internet — a LAN, a workshop, a boat, a building with no signal. /p2p needs nothing beyond the network you are standing on.
items.terminal: You live in a terminal and want chat to be one of the windows: scriptable, themeable, and extensible like everything else there.
items.yours: You want to run the server yourself, read all of it, and register with nothing at all — no phone number, no email, no account.

versus.close: Both can be true on the same day. Being direct about it costs nothing, and a project that claims to beat Signal is telling you something about its judgement.

controls.title: The commands you hope never to need
controls.lead: Most of CipherMesh protects the conversation. This part protects the person holding the laptop.

panic.name: Wipe everything, right now
panic.body: Session, history, trust store and keys are erased from disk and the client exits. There is no undo, and that is exactly the point.

lock.name: Locks itself when you walk away
lock.body: The screen goes behind your passphrase after the idle time you set. Type /lock to do it immediately.

ephemeral.name: Messages with an expiry date
ephemeral.body: Set a lifetime and everything sent from then on disappears from both ends when it runs out.

retention.name: Keep only what you meant to keep
retention.body: Anything older than the window you choose is wiped from disk. History exists at all only if you opened the session with a passphrase.

controls.note: None of this needs a server's cooperation. Every one of these is your own client acting on your own machine.

plugins.title: Any command you wish existed
plugins.lead: A slash command the client does not recognise is handed to your plugins. A plugin is one small ES module in ~/.ciphermesh/plugins — that file is the entire API.

send.name: Answer straight into the room
send.body: A handler that returns send posts its text into the room, through the same end-to-end encrypted path as anything you type. One that returns info shows it to you alone.

offline.name: Runs peer-to-peer too
offline.body: The same file works in P2P mode, where there is no server involved at all. Nothing about a plugin depends on a relay.

local.name: Nothing is ever downloaded
local.body: CipherMesh does not sync, fetch or auto-update plugins. The only way code reaches that folder is you putting it there.

warn.name: No sandbox — read it before you run it
warn.body: A plugin is arbitrary JavaScript inside your chat process, with access to your keys in memory. Treat a plugin file the way you treat curl | sh: install only what you wrote or read line by line.

open.title: Free, and open all the way down
open.lead: CipherMesh costs nothing and always will. The source is public under the MIT license — including the cryptography, which is exactly the part you should never have to take on faith.
open.auditBody: Every claim on this page is checkable in the repository. The protocol and threat model are documented in full.
open.contributeBody: Found a bug, want a feature, disagree with a design decision? Open an issue. Pull requests are welcome too — the contributing guide covers the workflow.

support.title: Support the project
support.lead: CipherMesh is built and maintained in spare time, and the public hub runs on a server that costs real money every month. If it is useful to you, a coffee helps keep both going.
support.note: Entirely optional. Nothing in CipherMesh is paywalled, and nothing ever will be.

notFound.title: That page is not here
notFound.body: The path you asked for does not exist on this site. If a link brought you here, it was pointing at something that was never published.

error.title: This page failed to render
error.body: Something broke on this end, not yours. Reloading usually clears it. If it keeps happening, an issue with what you were doing is genuinely useful.

meta.description: Whether the CipherMesh hub and the data this site reads are healthy right now.

status.title: Is anything broken?
status.notMeasured: Measured from this server, at the moment you loaded the page — nothing here is cached. Two things it cannot check: the WebSocket upgrade itself, which needs a real handshake rather than an HTTP request, and the certificate.
status.monitor: Both of those are watched every ten minutes from GitHub rather than from the machine they watch, because a monitor hosted on the box it is monitoring dies with it:
status.privacy: The relay line reports a range, never an exact count. An exact live number would let anyone reloading this page watch individual people arrive and leave — which is precisely the metadata the relay exists to withhold.
